newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rogue dissident join Cambodian army.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rogue dissident join Cambodian army.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen predicted on Wednesday that Khmer Rouge hardliners would be wiped out by mid-1997 as 2,500 defectors from the hardline Maoist group were officially welcomed into the Cambodian army.
"I think by half (mid-) 1997, Anlong Veng will be finished," the second prime minister told Reuters in Phnom Penh shortly before a welcoming ceremony for the breakaway fighters in the northwest.
Anlong Veng, located near the Thai border, is the jungle base of hardline guerrillas loyal to Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot.

Ieng Sary, leader of the breakaway Khmer Rouge faction, said Pol Pot has become concerned about dissenters within the hardline ranks. He said he suspected Pol Pot had one cadre, Mit Phort, killed in a bomb attack because the Khmer Rouge leader believed Mit Phort was a traitor.

Around 700 breakaway Khmer Rouge troops under Ieng Sary, representing the 2,500 defectors and 17,000 family members, received Cambodian army uniforms and new weapons at their northwestern base of Pailin in a ceremony that officially welded the former bitter enemies into the same fighting force.
"I am still a soldier, and I joined the Khmer Rouge army 20 years ago," said 70-year-old Chorn Reoun. "I am very pleased we have no more fighting ... and I will probably retire."
But Ieng Sary said Pol Pot and his commanders Ta Mok and Son Senn were in Anlong Veng preparing to attack Pailin and Phnom Malai.
"They are still preparing to fight. Pol Pot makes the orders directly," he said.
Ei Chien, the breakaway Khmer Rouge commander of Pailin, appealed to Pol Pot's hardliners to surrender their arms.

"May we seize this opportunity to appeal to our brother cadres and combatants and the dictatorial and fascist command of stubborn groups ... to stop spilling blood between Khmer and Khmer," he said in a statement.
Ieng Sary said he was tending to Pol Pot's ailing first wife, Khieu Ponnary, at his home in nearby Phnom Malai. Ieng Sary is married to Khieu Ponnary's sister, Khieu Thirith.
Co-Minister of Defence Tea Banh said he believed there were about 1,000 remaining Khmer Rouge hardliners, while a Western military analyst put their ranks at 2,000.

A second ceremony for several hundred more dissident guerrillas is planned for Thursday, when fighters from the nearby base of Phnom Malai will also trade in their Mao caps and worn fatigues for stiff new government-issue garb.

In August Ieng Sary's Pailin and Phnom Malai guerrillas broke with hardliners loyal to Pol Pot, whose brutal 1975-1979 regime was responsible for the deaths of more than one million Cambodians from starvation, disease or overwork.
Weeks of delicate negotiations ensued, with Cambodian co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen often competing to gain the upper hand, analysts said.

But in the end it was Hun Sen who recruited thousands of defectors directly to the government's ranks, cutting into Ieng Sary's potential base of support and leaving the rebel leader little bargaining power, analysts said.
Ei Chien steered clear of the spats in his statement, noting the former Khmer Rouge would not take on a political role in coming elections.
